Done. Here’s what I set up.

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns), 2 replicas
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80
  - Security config: matched stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both stable and canary. Port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080).

Why this gives ~50% traffic to canary
- The Service now selects 4 pods total (2 stable + 2 canary). With sessionAffinity=None, kube-proxy load-balances roughly evenly across all endpoints, resulting in about 50/50 traffic.

Current status
- engine-v2-1 Deployment is Ready with 2/2 replicas.
- Service endpoints include both deployments (4 addresses):
  - Stable: engine-v2-0-d99685f59-fgz7g, engine-v2-0-d99685f59-t6qcx
  - Canary: engine-v2-1-7994887c57-c848w, engine-v2-1-7994887c57-lptk7
- Service port remains 80 -> 8080.

Notes and next steps
- If you want a different split, change replica counts (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ≈ 25% canary).
- Rollback options:
  - Point Service back to only stable: set selector to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0
  - Or scale canary to 0 replicas.

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I set up.

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns), 2 replicas
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80
  - Security config: matched stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both stable and canary. Port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080).

Why this gives ~50% traffic to canary
- The Service now selects 4 pods total (2 stable + 2 canary). With sessionAffinity=None, kube-proxy load-balances roughly evenly across all endpoints, resulting in about 50/50 traffic.

Current status
- engine-v2-1 Deployment is Ready with 2/2 replicas.
- Service endpoints include both deployments (4 addresses):
  - Stable: engine-v2-0-d99685f59-fgz7g, engine-v2-0-d99685f59-t6qcx
  - Canary: engine-v2-1-7994887c57-c848w, engine-v2-1-7994887c57-lptk7
- Service port remains 80 -> 8080.

Notes and next steps
- If you want a different split, change replica counts (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ≈ 25% canary).
- Rollback options:
  - Point Service back to only stable: set selector to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0
  - Or scale canary to 0 replicas.

Done. Here’s what I set up.

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns), 2 replicas
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container name: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80
  - Security config: matched stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both stable and canary. Port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080).

Why this gives ~50% traffic to canary
- The Service now selects 4 pods total (2 stable + 2 canary). With sessionAffinity=None, kube-proxy load-balances roughly evenly across all endpoints, resulting in about 50/50 traffic.

Current status
- engine-v2-1 Deployment is Ready with 2/2 replicas.
- Service endpoints include both deployments (4 addresses):
  - Stable: engine-v2-0-d99685f59-fgz7g, engine-v2-0-d99685f59-t6qcx
  - Canary: engine-v2-1-7994887c57-c848w, engine-v2-1-7994887c57-lptk7
- Service port remains 80 -> 8080.

Notes and next steps
- If you want a different split, change replica counts (e.g., 3 stable + 1 canary ≈ 25% canary).
- Rollback options:
  - Point Service back to only stable: set selector to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0
  - Or scale canary to 0 replicas.

I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Event: ProvisioningFailed — storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC using the default StorageClass "standard".

Result
- PVC provisioned successfully and bound.
- homepage-pod is now Running and Ready in homepage-ns.

If you intended a different StorageClass, tell me the correct name and I’ll update the PVC. To avoid this in the future, you can also omit storageClassName to use the default class.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Event: ProvisioningFailed — storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC using the default StorageClass "standard".
  - Safe to delete: the PVC was never bound, so no data loss.

Result
- PVC provisioned successfully and bound.
- homepage-pod is now Running and Ready in homepage-ns.

If you intended a different StorageClass, tell me the correct name and I’ll update the PVC. To avoid this in the future, you can also omit storageClassName to use the default class.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Event: ProvisioningFailed — storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC using the default StorageClass "standard".
  - Safe to delete: the PVC was never bound, so no data loss.

Result
- PVC provisioned successfully and bound.
- homepage-pod is now Running and Ready in homepage-ns.

If you intended a different StorageClass, tell me the correct name and I’ll update the PVC. To avoid this in the future, you can also omit storageClassName to use the default class.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Probes were hitting port 80 on paths /get_status and /is_ready (which don’t exist), causing connection refused and restarts.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the app.
- Result: Pod was in CrashLoopBackOff and never became Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Ready and Running (orders/webapp-6b44c6f888-vw88q).
- Service: orders/webapp now forwards port 80 -> 8080 correctly.
- No new warning events; app is healthy.

How to test
- Port-forward: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
- Then: curl http://localhost:8080/ (should return the NGINX welcome page)

If you need external access, I can create an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Probes were hitting port 80 on paths /get_status and /is_ready (which don’t exist), causing connection refused and restarts.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the app.
- Result: Pod was in CrashLoopBackOff and never became Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Ready and Running (orders/webapp-6b44c6f888-vw88q).
- Service: orders/webapp now forwards port 80 -> 8080 correctly.
- No new warning events; app is healthy.

How to test
- Port-forward: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
- Then: curl http://localhost:8080/ (should return the NGINX welcome page)

If you need external access, I can create an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Probes were hitting port 80 on paths /get_status and /is_ready (which don’t exist), causing connection refused and restarts.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the app.
- Result: Pod was in CrashLoopBackOff and never became Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to use HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Ready and Running (orders/webapp-6b44c6f888-vw88q).
- Service: orders/webapp now forwards port 80 -> 8080 correctly.
- No new warning events; app is healthy.

How to test
- Port-forward: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
- Then: curl http://localhost:8080/ (should return the NGINX welcome page)

If you need external access, I can create an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service.

pod/webapp-6b44c6f888-vw88q condition met
Success: Pod is now Ready
Current liveness probe path: /

Success: Both probe paths have been fixed
Success: Pod is stable with acceptable number of restarts

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account didn’t grant permissions on pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments, so listing core/v1 pods was denied.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["list"]
- Kept the existing apps/deployments list permission and the RoleBinding as-is.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or try: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Optional
- If you also want to watch or get pods (common for UIs or controllers), I can add verbs: ["get","list","watch"].

Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account didn’t grant permissions on pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments, so listing core/v1 pods was denied.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["list"]
- Kept the existing apps/deployments list permission and the RoleBinding as-is.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- Or try: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Optional
- If you also want to watch or get pods (common for UIs or controllers), I can add verbs: ["get","list","watch"].

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the pod labels.
  - Service nginx (type ClusterIP) was selecting app=web.
  - The Deployment/pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service couldn’t reach any pods.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the pods:
  - selector: app=nginx
- Verified the fix:
  - Endpoints now show 10.244.0.25:8080 for Service nginx.
  - EndpointSlice is populated with port 8080.
  - In-pod test curl to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80/ returned HTTP 200.

Current status
- The nginx Service is now reachable inside the cluster via:
  - DNS: nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80
  - ClusterIP: 10.98.189.216:80

Notes on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP, which is internal-only. If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on each node’s IP at a fixed port.
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud or MetalLB).
  - Ingress: use an ingress controller and create an Ingress for host/path-based routing.
  - Port-forward (for quick testing): kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80

Tell me which option you prefer and I can set it up.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the pod labels.
  - Service nginx (type ClusterIP) was selecting app=web.
  - The Deployment/pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service couldn’t reach any pods.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the pods:
  - selector: app=nginx
- Verified the fix:
  - Endpoints now show 10.244.0.25:8080 for Service nginx.
  - EndpointSlice is populated with port 8080.
  - In-pod test curl to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80/ returned HTTP 200.

Current status
- The nginx Service is now reachable inside the cluster via:
  - DNS: nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80
  - ClusterIP: 10.98.189.216:80

Notes on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP, which is internal-only. If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on each node’s IP at a fixed port.
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud or MetalLB).
  - Ingress: use an ingress controller and create an Ingress for host/path-based routing.
  - Port-forward (for quick testing): kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80

Tell me which option you prefer and I can set it up.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the pod labels.
  - Service nginx (type ClusterIP) was selecting app=web.
  - The Deployment/pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service couldn’t reach any pods.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the pods:
  - selector: app=nginx
- Verified the fix:
  - Endpoints now show 10.244.0.25:8080 for Service nginx.
  - EndpointSlice is populated with port 8080.
  - In-pod test curl to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80/ returned HTTP 200.

Current status
- The nginx Service is now reachable inside the cluster via:
  - DNS: nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80
  - ClusterIP: 10.98.189.216:80

Notes on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP, which is internal-only. If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on each node’s IP at a fixed port.
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud or MetalLB).
  - Ingress: use an ingress controller and create an Ingress for host/path-based routing.
  - Port-forward (for quick testing): kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80

Tell me which option you prefer and I can set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but your cluster’s single node does not have that label. As a result, pods were Pending with FailedScheduling and the Service had no endpoints, causing connection refused to web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Events: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Service endpoints initially: <none>
  - Node labels: no environment=production-gpu label on the only node.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.

Current state (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-dnj56 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vtxf8 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.28:80, 10.244.0.29:80
- In-pod check: HTTP request to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local/ succeeded.

Why the connection errors happened
- With pods unscheduled, the Service had no backing endpoints. Requests to the ClusterIP resulted in connection refused.

Options going forward
- If you do not need GPU-specific nodes, keep the Deployment without nodeSelector (what I have applied).
- If you do need to constrain pods:
  - Label the target node(s): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Then re-add nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu to the Deployment.

Nice-to-have hardening
- Consider adding readinessProbe on port 80 so the Service won’t route traffic until the container is truly ready.
- Optionally set resource requests/limits appropriate for your workload.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Re-apply a corrected nodeSelector after labeling nodes, or
- Add readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but your cluster’s single node does not have that label. As a result, pods were Pending with FailedScheduling and the Service had no endpoints, causing connection refused to web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Events: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Service endpoints initially: <none>
  - Node labels: no environment=production-gpu label on the only node.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.

Current state (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-dnj56 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vtxf8 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.28:80, 10.244.0.29:80
- In-pod check: HTTP request to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local/ succeeded.

Why the connection errors happened
- With pods unscheduled, the Service had no backing endpoints. Requests to the ClusterIP resulted in connection refused.

Options going forward
- If you do not need GPU-specific nodes, keep the Deployment without nodeSelector (what I have applied).
- If you do need to constrain pods:
  - Label the target node(s): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Then re-add nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu to the Deployment.

Nice-to-have hardening
- Consider adding readinessProbe on port 80 so the Service won’t route traffic until the container is truly ready.
- Optionally set resource requests/limits appropriate for your workload.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Re-apply a corrected nodeSelector after labeling nodes, or
- Add readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but your cluster’s single node does not have that label. As a result, pods were Pending with FailedScheduling and the Service had no endpoints, causing connection refused to web-app-service.
- Evidence:
  - Events: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Service endpoints initially: <none>
  - Node labels: no environment=production-gpu label on the only node.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.

Current state (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-dnj56 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vtxf8 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.28:80, 10.244.0.29:80
- In-pod check: HTTP request to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local/ succeeded.

Why the connection errors happened
- With pods unscheduled, the Service had no backing endpoints. Requests to the ClusterIP resulted in connection refused.

Options going forward
- If you do not need GPU-specific nodes, keep the Deployment without nodeSelector (what I have applied).
- If you do need to constrain pods:
  - Label the target node(s): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Then re-add nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu to the Deployment.

Nice-to-have hardening
- Consider adding readinessProbe on port 80 so the Service won’t route traffic until the container is truly ready.
- Optionally set resource requests/limits appropriate for your workload.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Re-apply a corrected nodeSelector after labeling nodes, or
- Add readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment.

I’ve set up the requested multi-tenant development environment. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie/dev-shared: env=dev (used by network policies)
  - staging: env=staging; prod: env=prod

RBAC
- Service accounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Full access in own namespace:
  - Created a namespaced Role “namespace-owner” with full verbs on all resources in each dev namespace
  - Bound both the user and their service account to that Role:
    - dev-alice: RoleBinding rb-alice-owner → subjects: user alice; SA dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob: RoleBinding rb-bob-owner → subjects: user bob; SA dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: RoleBinding rb-charlie-owner → subjects: user charlie; SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding rb-devs-view in dev-shared: binds ClusterRole view to users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created. Only cluster-admins (via your existing cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding) can access.

Resource quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2; Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi; Pods 10; Services 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4; Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi; Pods 20; Services 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8; Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi; Pods 50; Services 20

Network policies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces:
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow within-namespace traffic:
  - allow-same-namespace policy (Ingress+Egress) in each namespace
- Developers can only access own namespace and dev-shared:
  - In dev namespaces: allow egress only to dev-shared
  - In dev-shared: allow ingress only from env=dev namespaces
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked (no inter-namespace rules between dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie)
- Allow DNS and system services:
  - Per-namespace egress to kube-system/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
  - Per-namespace general egress to kube-system (for system components)
- Staging/prod isolated from dev:
  - Default deny + allow-same-namespace only; no rules allowing traffic to/from dev
- Default deny applied everywhere except system namespaces (no policies were created in kube-system)

Notes and recommendations
- NetworkPolicy enforcement requires a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave Net). Ensure your cluster CNI enforces these.
- ServiceAccount tokens: if you need to use the developer service accounts from CI or outside-cluster, generate projected tokens or create Secrets per your cluster security policies (K8s 1.24+ uses bound tokens).
- You can further restrict the “namespace-owner” Role if you want to exclude certain sensitive resource types; current setup grants full rights within each dev namespace as requested.

How to verify
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns
- RBAC (as each user or impersonating):
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n staging --as charlie  (should be “no”)
- Quotas:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-shared
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n staging
- Network policies:
  - Deploy a test pod in each namespace (e.g., kubectl run -n dev-alice tmp --image=busybox:1.36 --sleep 3600 --restart=Never)
  - From dev-alice, curl to a Service in dev-shared (should work)
  - From dev-alice to dev-bob (should fail)
  - From any dev namespace to staging/prod (should fail)
  - DNS resolution from each namespace (should work)

Everything above has been applied to the cluster. If you want, I can export a single consolidated manifest containing all created objects for version control.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

I’ve set up the requested multi-tenant development environment. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie/dev-shared: env=dev (used by network policies)
  - staging: env=staging; prod: env=prod

RBAC
- Service accounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Full access in own namespace:
  - Created a namespaced Role “namespace-owner” with full verbs on all resources in each dev namespace
  - Bound both the user and their service account to that Role:
    - dev-alice: RoleBinding rb-alice-owner → subjects: user alice; SA dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob: RoleBinding rb-bob-owner → subjects: user bob; SA dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: RoleBinding rb-charlie-owner → subjects: user charlie; SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding rb-devs-view in dev-shared: binds ClusterRole view to users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created. Only cluster-admins (via your existing cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding) can access.

Resource quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2; Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi; Pods 10; Services 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4; Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi; Pods 20; Services 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8; Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi; Pods 50; Services 20

Network policies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces:
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow within-namespace traffic:
  - allow-same-namespace policy (Ingress+Egress) in each namespace
- Developers can only access own namespace and dev-shared:
  - In dev namespaces: allow egress only to dev-shared
  - In dev-shared: allow ingress only from env=dev namespaces
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked (no inter-namespace rules between dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie)
- Allow DNS and system services:
  - Per-namespace egress to kube-system/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
  - Per-namespace general egress to kube-system (for system components)
- Staging/prod isolated from dev:
  - Default deny + allow-same-namespace only; no rules allowing traffic to/from dev
- Default deny applied everywhere except system namespaces (no policies were created in kube-system)

Notes and recommendations
- NetworkPolicy enforcement requires a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave Net). Ensure your cluster CNI enforces these.
- ServiceAccount tokens: if you need to use the developer service accounts from CI or outside-cluster, generate projected tokens or create Secrets per your cluster security policies (K8s 1.24+ uses bound tokens).
- You can further restrict the “namespace-owner” Role if you want to exclude certain sensitive resource types; current setup grants full rights within each dev namespace as requested.

How to verify
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns
- RBAC (as each user or impersonating):
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n staging --as charlie  (should be “no”)
- Quotas:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-shared
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n staging
- Network policies:
  - Deploy a test pod in each namespace (e.g., kubectl run -n dev-alice tmp --image=busybox:1.36 --sleep 3600 --restart=Never)
  - From dev-alice, curl to a Service in dev-shared (should work)
  - From dev-alice to dev-bob (should fail)
  - From any dev namespace to staging/prod (should fail)
  - DNS resolution from each namespace (should work)

Everything above has been applied to the cluster. If you want, I can export a single consolidated manifest containing all created objects for version control.

outputSteps.content:
I’ve set up the requested multi-tenant development environment. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie/dev-shared: env=dev (used by network policies)
  - staging: env=staging; prod: env=prod

RBAC
- Service accounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Full access in own namespace:
  - Created a namespaced Role “namespace-owner” with full verbs on all resources in each dev namespace
  - Bound both the user and their service account to that Role:
    - dev-alice: RoleBinding rb-alice-owner → subjects: user alice; SA dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob: RoleBinding rb-bob-owner → subjects: user bob; SA dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: RoleBinding rb-charlie-owner → subjects: user charlie; SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding rb-devs-view in dev-shared: binds ClusterRole view to users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created. Only cluster-admins (via your existing cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding) can access.

Resource quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2; Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi; Pods 10; Services 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4; Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi; Pods 20; Services 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8; Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi; Pods 50; Services 20

Network policies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces:
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow within-namespace traffic:
  - allow-same-namespace policy (Ingress+Egress) in each namespace
- Developers can only access own namespace and dev-shared:
  - In dev namespaces: allow egress only to dev-shared
  - In dev-shared: allow ingress only from env=dev namespaces
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked (no inter-namespace rules between dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie)
- Allow DNS and system services:
  - Per-namespace egress to kube-system/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
  - Per-namespace general egress to kube-system (for system components)
- Staging/prod isolated from dev:
  - Default deny + allow-same-namespace only; no rules allowing traffic to/from dev
- Default deny applied everywhere except system namespaces (no policies were created in kube-system)

Notes and recommendations
- NetworkPolicy enforcement requires a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave Net). Ensure your cluster CNI enforces these.
- ServiceAccount tokens: if you need to use the developer service accounts from CI or outside-cluster, generate projected tokens or create Secrets per your cluster security policies (K8s 1.24+ uses bound tokens).
- You can further restrict the “namespace-owner” Role if you want to exclude certain sensitive resource types; current setup grants full rights within each dev namespace as requested.

How to verify
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns
- RBAC (as each user or impersonating):
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n staging --as charlie  (should be “no”)
- Quotas:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-shared
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n staging
- Network policies:
  - Deploy a test pod in each namespace (e.g., kubectl run -n dev-alice tmp --image=busybox:1.36 --sleep 3600 --restart=Never)
  - From dev-alice, curl to a Service in dev-shared (should work)
  - From dev-alice to dev-bob (should fail)
  - From any dev namespace to staging/prod (should fail)
  - DNS resolution from each namespace (should work)

Everything above has been applied to the cluster. If you want, I can export a single consolidated manifest containing all created objects for version control.
